source.title: Understand Depression
source.attribution: A Reborn guide drawing on the NHS, the National Institute of Mental Health, the World Health Organization, NICE and Mind.
source.notes: Written by Reborn; no text copied. References: NHS, Depression in adults: overview, https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/depression-in-adults/overview/; National Institute of Mental Health, Depression, https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/depression; World Health Organization, Depressive disorder (depression) fact sheet, https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/depression; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, Depression in adults: treatment and management (NG222), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng222; Mind, Depression, https://www.mind.org.uk/information-support/types-of-mental-health-problems/depression/about-depression/

cards.title: Depression is a common, real and treatable health condition
cards.body:
This guide explains what depression is, how it differs from ordinary sadness, and what helps. It covers the signs, the many possible causes, common myths, talking therapies, the basics of medication, and everyday steps such as behavioural activation, sleep and movement.

Depression is not a choice and it is not a weakness. Health bodies such as the NHS and the World Health Organization describe it as a common condition that affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide, and most people get better with the right support.

This guide is general information, not a diagnosis. If you are worried about yourself or someone else, a doctor is a good first step. If anyone is in danger right now, contact local emergency services or a crisis line.
cards.apply_it: Note one question you hope this guide will answer for you, and keep it in mind as you read.

quiz.question: Which statement about depression is most accurate?
options: It is a sign of a weak character
It is a common health condition that usually improves with support
It only affects people with hard lives
It always goes away on its own in a week
quiz.explanation: Depression is a recognised health condition. It is common, it can affect anyone, and most people recover with the right help.

cards.title: Sadness comes and goes, while depression lingers and spreads
cards.body:
Everyone feels sad sometimes. A bad day at work, a row with a friend or a disappointing result can leave you low for a while. Ordinary sadness usually has a clear cause, eases with time, and still lets you enjoy some things, like a funny film or a meal with friends.

Depression is different. The low mood or loss of interest lasts most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. It can show up with no obvious reason. It tends to spread into sleep, energy, appetite, work and relationships, and things that used to bring joy can feel flat or pointless.

If low feelings are sticking around and getting in the way of daily life, that is a good reason to talk to a doctor.
cards.apply_it: Think back over the last two weeks. On how many days did low mood or lack of interest last most of the day?

quiz.question: Which feature points more towards depression than ordinary sadness?
options: Feeling down after an argument, then cheering up
Crying at a sad film
Low mood most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more
Feeling disappointed about a cancelled trip
quiz.explanation: Ordinary sadness passes. Depression lasts most of the day for at least two weeks and affects many parts of life.

cards.title: The core signs are low mood and losing interest in things
cards.body:
Doctors usually look for two main signs. The first is a low, sad, empty or hopeless mood. The second is losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, sometimes called anhedonia.

For example, someone who loved football might stop going to matches, not because they are busy, but because it no longer feels worth it. Someone else might still go through the motions but feel nothing.

Other emotional signs can include feeling tearful, irritable, numb or anxious. Some people feel guilty or worthless for no good reason. Not everyone feels sad: some mostly feel flat or cut off.

Having one of these feelings now and then is normal. It is the mix, the strength and how long it lasts that matter.
cards.apply_it: Write down three things you used to enjoy. Notice honestly whether they still feel the same.

quiz.question: What does the term anhedonia describe?
options: Losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy
Sleeping too much at weekends
Feeling very energetic
A fear of crowded places
quiz.explanation: Anhedonia means a loss of pleasure or interest. Along with low mood, it is one of the two core signs doctors look for.

cards.title: Depression often shows up in the body as well as the mind
cards.body:
Depression is not only about feelings. It often changes how the body works too.

Sleep can be hit in different ways: waking very early and lying awake, struggling to fall asleep, or sleeping far more than usual. Appetite and weight can drop or rise. Many people feel tired all the time, so that even a shower or answering a message feels like hard work.

Some people move or speak more slowly than usual, while others feel restless and unable to sit still. Aches, headaches and stomach problems without a clear cause are also common.

Because other health problems, such as an underactive thyroid, can cause some of the same signs, a doctor may suggest checks to rule them out.
cards.apply_it: For one week, jot down your sleep, energy and appetite each day in a few words.

quiz.question: Why might a doctor suggest blood tests when someone has signs of depression?
options: Blood tests can diagnose depression directly
To check for other health problems that cause similar signs
Because medication is always needed first
To measure how sad someone is
quiz.explanation: There is no blood test for depression itself, but conditions like thyroid problems can cause similar signs, so a doctor may check.

cards.title: Depression changes how you think, not just how you feel
cards.body:
Depression often affects thinking. Concentrating can become hard, so reading a page or following a TV plot feels like a struggle. Making small decisions, like what to eat, can feel overwhelming. Memory may seem worse.

Thoughts also tend to turn negative. A person might think, I always mess things up, nobody would miss me, or things will never get better. These thoughts feel like facts, but they are often symptoms of the illness speaking.

Some people start having thoughts of death or of ending their life. These thoughts are a sign of serious distress, not a character flaw, and they need attention. If you have them, please talk to a doctor soon, and if you feel unsafe, contact local emergency services or a crisis line now.
cards.apply_it: When a harsh thought appears, label it: that may be the depression talking.

quiz.question: How should thoughts like 'things will never get better' be understood during depression?
options: As proven facts about the future
As a sign of laziness
As something everyone ignores easily
As common symptoms of the illness that can feel true but often are not
quiz.explanation: Depression colours thinking. Hopeless thoughts feel real, but they are often symptoms that ease as the person recovers.

cards.title: Depression can look different in different people
cards.body:
There is no single face of depression. It can look quite different from person to person.

Some people, including many men, show it more through anger, irritability, working all hours, risky behaviour or drinking more, rather than tears. Teenagers may seem moody, snappy or withdrawn, and their school work may slip. Older adults may talk more about aches, tiredness or memory than about mood.

Some people with depression keep going to work, look after their children and smile in public, while struggling badly inside. This is sometimes called high-functioning depression, though it is not a formal diagnosis.

So it helps not to judge by appearances. Someone who seems fine may still need support.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone close to you. Have you noticed any lasting change in them, even a quiet one?

quiz.question: Which of these could be a sign of depression in some people?
options: Only crying in public
Being irritable, drinking more or working all hours
Always looking visibly sad
Never smiling at all
quiz.explanation: Depression does not always look like sadness. Irritability, anger, overwork and drinking more can all be ways it shows.

cards.title: Depression is very common and can affect anyone
cards.body:
The World Health Organization estimates that depression affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide, and it is one of the leading causes of disability. In many countries, a large share of people will have depression at some point in their life.

It can affect anyone: young or old, rich or poor, famous or not. People with good jobs and loving families can still get depressed. Women are diagnosed more often than men, though men may be less likely to seek help.

Knowing how common it is can ease feelings of shame. If you are struggling, you are far from alone, and many people who have been where you are now feel much better.
cards.apply_it: Remind yourself today: needing help for my mind is as normal as needing help for my body.

quiz.question: What does the WHO say about how common depression is?
options: It is very rare
It only affects older people
It affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide
It has almost disappeared
quiz.explanation: The WHO estimates that depression affects hundreds of millions of people globally and is a leading cause of disability.

cards.title: There is rarely one single cause of depression
cards.body:
Researchers think depression usually comes from a mix of things working together, and the mix is different for each person.

Biology plays a part. Depression can run in families, which suggests genes affect risk, but having a parent with depression does not mean you will get it. Hormone changes, long-term illness, pain and some medicines can also raise the risk.

Life plays a part too. Stressful events, loss, loneliness, money worries, abuse or trauma, especially early in life, can all add to it.

Personality and habits of thinking, such as being very self-critical, may make some people more vulnerable. Often, several small pressures build up until they tip someone over.
cards.apply_it: List any pressures that have built up in your life this year, big or small, without judging them.

quiz.question: What is the best summary of what causes depression?
options: A mix of biology, life events and other factors, different for each person
Only bad parenting
Only a lack of willpower
Only genes, so nothing else matters
quiz.explanation: Most experts see depression as coming from several factors together, such as genes, health, stress and life events.

cards.title: The chemical imbalance idea is too simple
cards.body:
You may have heard that depression is caused by a chemical imbalance, such as too little serotonin. This idea was popular for many years, but scientists now see it as too simple.

The brain is complex. Depression seems to involve changes in many systems, including how brain areas communicate, how the body handles stress, inflammation, and how the brain adapts over time. Exactly how these fit together is still being studied and debated.

This does not mean depression is not real or that medicine does not help. Antidepressants do help many people, even though scientists do not fully understand why. It simply means that depression is not one thing with one fix.
cards.apply_it: If someone tells you depression is just low serotonin, gently share that the science is more complex.

quiz.question: What do scientists currently think about the chemical imbalance explanation?
options: It is proven and complete
It means medication cannot work
It shows depression is not real
It is too simple, and depression involves many brain and body systems
quiz.explanation: Research suggests depression involves many systems. The simple chemical imbalance story does not capture it, though treatments can still help.

cards.title: Depression ranges from mild to severe and has several forms
cards.body:
Doctors often describe depression as less severe or more severe, depending on how many signs a person has and how much they affect daily life.

There are also particular forms. Postnatal depression can develop in the year after having a baby, and it can affect both mothers and fathers. Seasonal affective disorder follows the seasons, often worse in winter. Persistent depressive disorder is a long-lasting, lower-level depression that can go on for years.

Low mood is also part of bipolar disorder, where periods of depression alternate with periods of very high mood or energy. This needs different treatment, so it is important to tell a doctor if you have ever had times of unusually high energy.
cards.apply_it: If you have ever had spells of unusually high energy or little need for sleep, note them to mention to a doctor.

quiz.question: Why is it important to tell a doctor about past periods of very high mood or energy?
options: It proves there is no depression
It may point to bipolar disorder, which needs different treatment
It means you need no help
Doctors never ask about mood
quiz.explanation: Bipolar disorder includes highs as well as lows and is treated differently, so doctors need to know about any past highs.

cards.title: You cannot simply snap out of depression
cards.body:
One of the most common myths is that a depressed person could just cheer up, try harder or think positively. If only it were that easy.

Depression is a health condition, not a mood someone has chosen. Telling a depressed person to snap out of it is a bit like telling someone with a broken leg to walk it off. It usually makes them feel more guilty and alone.

What does help is a mix of support, treatment and small, steady steps, which are described later in this guide. People do play an active part in their recovery, but they need patience and help, not pressure.

If you catch yourself thinking you should just get over it, try treating yourself with the kindness you would give a friend.
cards.apply_it: Replace one 'I should just get over it' thought with 'I am unwell, and I am taking steps to get better.'

quiz.question: Why is telling someone to 'snap out of it' unhelpful?
options: Because depression is not a choice and pressure can add guilt
Because depression always lasts forever
Because people with depression cannot change anything
Because it is too polite
quiz.explanation: Depression is not chosen. Pressure to cheer up usually adds guilt, while support and small steps help much more.

cards.title: Depression is not weakness and does not need a reason
cards.body:
Another myth is that only weak people get depressed. In reality, many strong, capable and successful people have had depression. Getting help takes courage.

A related myth is that you need a good reason to be depressed. People sometimes say, but your life is good, what do you have to be sad about? Depression can appear even when life looks fine from the outside, because biology and hidden pressures play a part.

Yet another myth is that talking about it makes it worse. For most people, talking to someone they trust or to a professional is a relief and an important step towards feeling better.
cards.apply_it: If you feel ashamed, write one sentence explaining your situation to yourself as you would to a good friend.

quiz.question: Which of these is a myth about depression?
options: Depression can appear when life seems fine
Strong people can get depressed
You need an obvious reason to be depressed
Talking about it often helps
quiz.explanation: Depression can happen without a clear trigger. Needing a good reason is a myth that can stop people asking for help.

cards.title: Grief and depression can look alike but are not the same
cards.body:
After someone dies, or after another big loss, deep sadness is natural. Grief can bring crying, poor sleep, low appetite and trouble focusing, just like depression.

There are some differences. In grief, pain often comes in waves, mixed with warm memories and even moments of laughter. Self-worth usually stays steady. In depression, the low mood is more constant, and feelings of worthlessness or self-blame are common.

Grief and depression can also happen together. If grief stays very intense for a long time, stops you functioning, or comes with thoughts of not wanting to live, please talk to a doctor. Support is available and it is never too soon or too late to ask.
cards.apply_it: If you are grieving, plan one small way to remember the person kindly this week.

quiz.question: Which is more typical of depression than of ordinary grief?
options: Waves of sadness mixed with warm memories
Missing the person who died
Crying on anniversaries
A constant low mood with feelings of worthlessness
quiz.explanation: Grief often comes in waves and keeps self-worth steady. Constant low mood and worthlessness point more towards depression.

cards.title: See a doctor if low mood lasts two weeks or more
cards.body:
It is a good idea to see a doctor if you have felt low, empty or uninterested in things most days for more than two weeks, or if your mood is getting in the way of work, study, relationships or looking after yourself.

You do not need to be sure it is depression. You do not need to be in crisis. Doctors would much rather see people early, when things are often easier to treat.

See someone urgently if you have thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life. If you feel you might act on these thoughts, or you are not safe right now, contact local emergency services or a crisis line straight away.
cards.apply_it: If your low mood has lasted two weeks, book an appointment with a doctor this week.

quiz.question: When is a good time to see a doctor about low mood?
options: Only after several years
When it has lasted two weeks or more, or is affecting daily life
Only when you are completely sure it is depression
Never, it is better to wait
quiz.explanation: Health services advise seeing a doctor when low mood lasts over two weeks or affects life. You do not need to be certain or in crisis.

cards.title: A doctor's visit about mood is a normal conversation
cards.body:
Many people worry about what will happen at the appointment. Usually it is simply a talk.

The doctor may ask how you have been feeling, how long it has lasted, how you are sleeping and eating, and what is going on in your life. They might use a short questionnaire to understand how strong your symptoms are. They will usually ask, kindly, whether you have had thoughts of harming yourself, because this helps them keep you safe.

They may suggest tests to rule out other causes. Then you can talk through options together, such as self-help, talking therapy or medication.

It can help to write notes beforehand, because it is easy to forget things or play them down on the day.
cards.apply_it: Write three lines before your appointment: how you feel, how long it has lasted, and what it stops you doing.

quiz.question: Why might a doctor ask about thoughts of self-harm?
options: To help keep you safe and plan the right support
To get you into trouble
Because they think you are lying
It is just a formality with no purpose
quiz.explanation: Asking about self-harm is a normal, caring part of an assessment. It helps the doctor understand risk and offer the right support.

cards.title: Talking therapies help many people with depression
cards.body:
Talking therapies are a main treatment for depression. Guidelines such as those from NICE in the UK recommend them for many people, including as a first option for less severe depression.

Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, is one of the best studied. It looks at the links between thoughts, feelings and actions. You learn to notice unhelpful thinking patterns, test them against the evidence, and try small changes in what you do.

For example, if you think, my friends do not want to see me, you might test that by sending one message and seeing what happens.

Therapy can be one to one, in groups, online or guided self-help. It takes some effort, but the skills can last.
cards.apply_it: Find out how talking therapy is accessed where you live, for example through a doctor or a self-referral service.

quiz.question: What does CBT mainly focus on?
options: Analysing dreams only
The links between thoughts, feelings and actions
Avoiding all feelings
Taking medication on time
quiz.explanation: CBT looks at how thoughts, feelings and behaviour affect each other, and teaches practical ways to change unhelpful patterns.

cards.title: There are several kinds of talking therapy to choose from
cards.body:
CBT is not the only option. Guidelines describe several talking therapies that can help with depression.

Behavioural activation focuses on slowly getting back to meaningful and enjoyable activities. Interpersonal therapy looks at relationships and life changes, like a breakup or a new role. Counselling gives space to talk through problems with a trained listener. Some people use guided self-help, working through a book or online course with support from a practitioner. Group therapy and mindfulness-based therapy can also help, especially in preventing relapse.

No single therapy suits everyone. A good fit with your therapist matters a lot. If one approach does not feel right, it is fine to say so and ask about others.
cards.apply_it: Look up two types of talking therapy and note which one sounds most like a fit for you.

quiz.question: Which therapy focuses mainly on relationships and life changes?
options: Behavioural activation
Guided self-help
Interpersonal therapy
Physiotherapy
quiz.explanation: Interpersonal therapy focuses on relationships and life transitions, which can play a big part in depression.

cards.title: Antidepressants can help, and they take time to work
cards.body:
Antidepressants are medicines that can help ease depression, especially when it is more severe or has not improved with other help. There are several types, and a doctor will talk through which might suit you.

A few general points are worth knowing. They usually take a few weeks to start helping, so it is common to feel no change at first. Some people have side effects, such as nausea or sleep changes, which often ease after a while. Antidepressants are not addictive in the way some drugs are, but stopping suddenly can cause unpleasant effects.

Always talk to your doctor before starting, changing or stopping a medicine. They can adjust the dose or try another one if needed.
cards.apply_it: If you take an antidepressant, write down any questions or side effects to discuss at your next review.

quiz.question: What is true about antidepressants in general?
options: They work within an hour
You should stop them suddenly when you feel better
They are the only treatment for depression
They often take a few weeks to start working
quiz.explanation: Antidepressants usually take some weeks to help. Changes to them should always be made with a doctor's advice.

cards.title: Treatment is often a mix, and finding the right fit can take time
cards.body:
Many people do best with a combination of approaches: perhaps therapy plus medication, along with changes to daily routine and support from friends.

It is normal if the first thing you try is not the perfect answer. A therapy might not click, or a medicine might cause side effects. This is not failure. It is useful information that helps you and your doctor find a better fit.

Recovery is rarely a straight line. There may be good weeks and bad weeks. Keeping a simple mood diary can help you see slow progress that is hard to notice day to day.

Keep talking honestly with the people treating you. Tell them what is and is not helping.
cards.apply_it: Start a simple daily mood score from 1 to 10, with one line about your day.

quiz.question: If the first treatment does not help much, what is the best response?
options: Give up on all treatment
Tell your doctor or therapist, so you can try a better fit
Double the dose without asking
Assume you cannot recover
quiz.explanation: Finding the right treatment can take a few tries. Honest feedback helps professionals adjust the plan.

cards.title: Depression shrinks life, and a shrinking life feeds depression
cards.body:
When you feel low and tired, it is natural to pull back. You cancel plans, stop hobbies and stay in bed longer. In the short term, this can feel like relief.

But over time, a smaller life means fewer moments of pleasure, achievement and connection. That can deepen the low mood, which makes you pull back even more. Experts describe this as a downward spiral.

Behavioural activation is a well-researched approach that works on this spiral. Instead of waiting to feel better before doing things, you gently start doing small, valued things, and the mood often follows.

The next few cards show how to try this yourself, alongside any professional help you have.
cards.apply_it: Write down two things you have stopped doing since your mood dropped.

quiz.question: What is the main idea of behavioural activation?
options: Gently doing small, valued activities to help mood follow
Resting in bed until you feel completely better
Avoiding all people
Working longer hours
quiz.explanation: Behavioural activation breaks the cycle of withdrawal by gently reintroducing activities, so that mood can follow action.

cards.title: Plan small activities that bring pleasure, achievement or meaning
cards.body:
To try behavioural activation, start by making a list of activities. Include three kinds: things that give a little pleasure, like listening to music; things that give a sense of achievement, like washing the dishes; and things that matter to you, like calling a relative.

Then pick very small versions. Not clean the house, but wash five plates. Not go for a run, but walk to the end of the street.

Schedule one or two into a specific time, such as Tuesday at 10am. Afterwards, rate your mood and how much the activity mattered, from 0 to 10.

Over days and weeks, slowly add more. Small, regular steps beat big plans that feel impossible.
cards.apply_it: Pick one tiny activity for tomorrow and write down the exact time you will do it.

quiz.question: Which is the best example of a behavioural activation step?
options: Clean the whole house today
Wait until you feel motivated
Walk to the end of the street at 10am on Tuesday
Plan a month of busy weekends
quiz.explanation: Small, specific and scheduled activities are easier to start and build confidence for the next step.

cards.title: Action often comes before motivation when you are depressed
cards.body:
People often wait to feel like doing something. With depression, that feeling may not come for a long time. Behavioural activation flips the order: you act first, in a tiny way, and motivation may follow.

For example, you may not feel like seeing a friend. But if you go for twenty minutes, you might come home feeling slightly lighter. Even if you do not enjoy it much, you have shown yourself that you can do it.

Expect some days to go badly. If you skip a planned activity, do not use it as proof that you are failing. Just pick the next small step and try again. Be as patient with yourself as you would be with a friend learning to walk after an injury.
cards.apply_it: Tell yourself: I do not have to feel like it, I only have to do two minutes of it.

quiz.question: With depression, what does behavioural activation suggest about motivation?
options: You must feel motivated before acting
Motivation never matters
Skipping one activity means you have failed
Small actions can come first, and motivation may follow
quiz.explanation: Waiting for motivation can keep people stuck. Taking a small step first often helps motivation and mood begin to return.

cards.title: Steady sleep habits support recovery from depression
cards.body:
Sleep and mood are closely linked. Depression can disturb sleep, and poor sleep can make low mood worse.

Some simple habits help many people. Try to get up at roughly the same time every day, even after a bad night, because this anchors your body clock. Get some daylight in the morning. Keep naps short and early. Cut down on caffeine after lunch and avoid using alcohol to fall asleep, as it disturbs sleep later in the night.

If you lie awake for a long time, get up and do something calm in dim light, then return to bed when sleepy.

If sleep problems are severe or lasting, talk to a doctor. There are effective treatments for insomnia that do not rely on sleeping pills.
cards.apply_it: Choose a fixed wake-up time and stick to it for the next seven days.

quiz.question: Which sleep habit is most helpful for mood?
options: Getting up at about the same time every day
Sleeping in late whenever possible
Drinking alcohol to fall asleep
Long afternoon naps every day
quiz.explanation: A regular wake time steadies the body clock. Alcohol and long naps tend to disrupt sleep further.

cards.title: Physical activity can lift mood, even in small amounts
cards.body:
Research shows that physical activity can help with depression, and guidelines such as NICE include group exercise as one option. It is not a cure on its own for everyone, but it can make a real difference.

You do not need a gym or special kit. A brisk walk, dancing in the kitchen, gardening or swimming all count. Activity outdoors, especially with other people, may bring extra benefits.

Start small. Five or ten minutes is a good beginning when energy is low. Gradually build up towards the general advice of about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, if your health allows.

If you have a health condition, check with a doctor about what is safe for you.
cards.apply_it: Take a ten-minute walk today, ideally outside in daylight.

quiz.question: What is a good way to start being active when you are depressed?
options: Run a marathon next week
Only exercise if you can do an hour
Start with five or ten minutes of something you can manage
Wait until you feel full of energy
quiz.explanation: Short, manageable bursts of activity are a realistic start and can be built up slowly.

cards.title: Food, alcohol and drugs all affect mood
cards.body:
When you feel low, it is easy to skip meals, live on snacks, or drink more to numb things. These habits can make mood worse over time.

Alcohol is a depressant. It may give brief relief, but it can deepen low mood, disrupt sleep, and make anxiety worse the next day. It can also interact with some medicines. Recreational drugs can have similar or stronger effects.

Regular meals help keep energy steadier. You do not need a perfect diet. Simple steps like eating breakfast, having some fruit and vegetables, and drinking enough water are a good start.

If you are relying on alcohol or drugs to cope, tell a doctor. Help is available without judgement.
cards.apply_it: Track how much alcohol you drink this week and note how you feel the next morning.

quiz.question: How does alcohol tend to affect depression?
options: It cures low mood
It may give brief relief but can deepen low mood and harm sleep
It has no effect on mood
It always improves sleep
quiz.explanation: Alcohol is a depressant. Brief relief is often followed by worse mood, poorer sleep and more anxiety.

cards.title: Staying connected is protective, even when you want to hide
cards.body:
Depression can make you want to hide away. You may feel like a burden, or think nobody wants to hear from you. But connection is one of the most protective things for mental health.

You do not have to share everything. You could start by telling one trusted person that you are having a hard time. Or simply spend time with someone without talking about your feelings at all, like watching a match together.

If talking feels too hard, a short text can work: I am finding things tough at the moment, could we meet up? Many people feel relieved to be asked.

Peer support groups, online or in person, can also help you feel less alone.
cards.apply_it: Send one short message to someone you trust today, even if it is just to say hello.

quiz.question: What is a good first step towards connection when you feel low?
options: Telling one trusted person you are finding things hard
Waiting until you feel fully better
Sharing everything with everyone at once
Cutting off all contact
quiz.explanation: Starting small, with one trusted person, makes connection less daunting and can bring real comfort.

cards.title: Gently questioning harsh thoughts can loosen their grip
cards.body:
Depression often brings a harsh inner voice: I am useless, I always fail, everyone is better than me. These thoughts can feel completely true.

One idea from CBT is to treat them as guesses rather than facts. When you notice one, ask yourself a few questions. What is the evidence for and against this? Would I say this to a friend? Is there another way of seeing it?

For example, I always fail might become, I did not get that job, but I have done well at other things. This is not about forcing positive thinking. It is about finding a fairer, more balanced view.

Writing thoughts down can make this easier. A therapist can teach these skills in more depth.
cards.apply_it: Write down one harsh thought today and next to it a fairer, more balanced version.

quiz.question: What does CBT suggest doing with harsh thoughts like 'I always fail'?
options: Believe them completely
Ignore all thoughts forever
Force yourself to think only happy thoughts
Treat them as guesses and look for a fairer view
quiz.explanation: CBT encourages checking thoughts against the evidence and finding a more balanced view, not forcing positivity.

cards.title: Depression can come back, so know your warning signs
cards.body:
Many people recover fully from depression. For some, it returns at a later time, which is called relapse. Knowing this is not meant to scare you. It helps you spot early signs and act quickly.

Early warning signs are personal. They might include sleeping badly, withdrawing from friends, losing interest in hobbies, feeling more irritable, or a return of self-critical thoughts.

A relapse plan can help. Write down your warning signs, what helped last time, who you can talk to, and when you will contact a doctor. Share it with someone you trust.

If you take medication, guidelines advise continuing it for a while after you feel better, to lower the risk of relapse. Talk to your doctor before stopping.
cards.apply_it: Write down three personal warning signs that your mood might be slipping.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to know your early warning signs?
options: They prove you will always be depressed
They mean treatment never works
They help you act quickly if depression starts to return
They are only useful to doctors
quiz.explanation: Spotting early signs means you can use your plan and get support sooner, which can stop a relapse from deepening.

cards.title: If you have thoughts of suicide, help is there right now
cards.body:
Thoughts of suicide can be part of depression. They can be frightening, and it can be hard to tell anyone. But you deserve support, and these feelings can pass with help.

If you feel you might act on these thoughts, or you are not safe, contact local emergency services or a crisis line now, or go to a hospital emergency department. If you can, stay with someone or ask someone to come to you.

If you are not in immediate danger but are struggling, tell someone you trust and contact your doctor soon. Try to put distance between yourself and anything you could use to harm yourself.

Many people who once felt this way go on to feel much better. Reaching out is a strong and brave step.
cards.apply_it: Save the number of a local crisis line in your phone today, so it is there if you or someone else needs it.

quiz.question: What should someone do if they feel they might act on thoughts of suicide?
options: Keep it secret and wait
Contact local emergency services or a crisis line straight away
Wait for their next routine appointment
Try to sleep it off alone
quiz.explanation: In a crisis, contacting emergency services or a crisis line straight away is the safest step. Staying with someone also helps.

cards.title: Recovery is possible, one small step at a time
cards.body:
Depression is a common, real health condition. It is more than sadness: it lasts, spreads into many parts of life, and can change how you think and feel about yourself. It usually comes from a mix of causes, and it is not your fault.

Help works. Talking therapies, medication when needed, behavioural activation, steady sleep, movement and connection all play a part. Recovery can take time and may have ups and downs, so be patient with yourself.

If low mood has lasted two weeks or more, talk to a doctor. If you or someone else is in danger, contact local emergency services or a crisis line straight away.

One small step today is enough.
cards.apply_it: Choose one idea from this guide and do the smallest possible version of it today.

quiz.question: Which summary of this guide is most accurate?
options: Depression is a choice that people can stop
Only medication can help depression
Nothing can be done until you feel better
Depression is a real condition, and a mix of support and small steps can help
quiz.explanation: Depression is treatable. Professional help, daily habits and connection all play a role, and small steps count.
